summary: This standards-track document defines the canonical syntax of Uniform Resource Names, which are meant to be persistent, location-independent identifiers for resources. It was replaced by RFC 8141.

plainLanguage.summary: A URN is a name for a resource that is meant to stay valid no matter where the resource moves to. RFC 2141 fixes the exact shape of such a name, says which characters are allowed, and explains how to encode the ones that are not. It also gives the test for deciding whether two differently written URNs name the same thing.

subtitle: The canonical shape of a Uniform Resource Name, and how two names are compared.

tldr.problem: A name for a resource is only useful if it keeps pointing at the same resource forever. A Uniform Resource Name is meant to do that, but only if every party writes it the same way and can tell when two spellings name the same thing.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2141 gives the canonical syntax of a URN as the literal prefix urn:, a namespace identifier, and a namespace specific string. It defines the characters allowed in each part, how characters outside the allowed set are percent-encoded, and a procedure for deciding whether two URNs are lexically equivalent.
tldr.outcome: The document also says how a URN should be displayed and transported, and that a URL resolver must treat a URN as an opaque name and hand it to a URN resolver. It was a Proposed Standard until it was obsoleted by RFC 8141.

facts.label: Escaped octet form
facts.value: A percent sign and two hexadecimal characters

facts.label: Case-insensitive parts
facts.value: The leading urn: token and the namespace identifier

today: RFC 2141 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 8141, which carries the current syntax for Uniform Resource Names.

sections.title: What a URN Is For
sections.content:
Uniform Resource Names are intended to serve as persistent, location-independent resource identifiers. Unlike a web address, which points at a place, a URN points at a thing and keeps pointing at it after the thing moves. The syntax is designed to make it easy to map other naming spaces that share these properties into URN space, and to encode character data in a form that can be sent in existing protocols and transcribed on most keyboards.

The document sets forward the canonical syntax for URNs. It also discusses the legacy and new namespaces that exist, the requirements for presenting and transporting URNs, and how to decide whether two URNs are the same.
sections.plainLanguage: A web address points at a place. A URN points at a thing, so it keeps working after the thing is moved. That is why libraries and other organisations use URNs for the things they catalogue.

sections.title: The Overall Syntax
sections.content:
Every URN has the same shape:

<URN> ::= "urn:" <NID> ":" <NSS>

The NID is the namespace identifier and the NSS is the namespace specific string. The leading urn: sequence is case insensitive. The namespace identifier determines the syntactic interpretation of the namespace specific string, so each namespace gets to say what its own strings look like.

The namespace identifier syntax is deliberately loose, so that it does not constrain any particular way of resolving names. It is a letter or a digit followed by up to 31 more characters, each of which is a letter, a digit or a hyphen. This is slightly more restrictive than the URL specification, which also allows the characters dot and plus. The namespace identifier is case insensitive, so ISBN and isbn name the same namespace.

To avoid confusion with the urn prefix itself, the namespace identifier urn is reserved and must not be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Every URN is the word urn, a colon, the name of its namespace, another colon, and then the part that namespace defines. The namespace name is short, at most 32 characters, and its case does not matter.

sections.title: The Namespace Specific String and Escaping
sections.content:
There is a single canonical representation of the namespace specific string, as required by RFC 1737. It is one or more URN characters, and a URN character is either a transmittable character or a percent sign followed by two hexadecimal digits.

The transmittable characters are letters, digits, a set of punctuation marks including the parentheses, comma, hyphen, dot, colon, equals sign, at sign, semicolon, dollar sign, underscore, exclamation mark, asterisk and apostrophe, and the reserved characters.

Valid identifiers in a namespace may contain characters outside that set. Such strings must be translated into the canonical form before they are used as protocol elements or passed to other applications. Translation encodes each character outside the set as a sequence of one to six octets using UTF-8, and writes each of those octets as a percent sign followed by the two hexadecimal characters that give its value.

The reserved characters are the percent sign itself, the forward slash, the question mark and the number sign. The percent sign introduces the escape sequence, so a literal percent sign in a namespace must be written as %25, and any percent sign in a URN must be followed by two characters from the hexadecimal set. The other three were reserved by RFC 1630 for particular purposes that the URN working group had not yet settled, so they are reserved for future developments and namespace developers should not use them unencoded.

The excluded characters are the octets 1 to 32, the octets 127 to 255, and the characters backslash, double quote, ampersand, less-than, greater-than, square brackets, circumflex, backtick, curly braces, vertical bar and tilde. Any of these must be percent-encoded if it is used in a URN, and octet 0 should never be used in either form. A URN ends when an excluded character is reached, and that character is not part of the URN.
sections.plainLanguage: Most punctuation can appear as it is. Anything else is written as a percent sign and two hexadecimal digits, which is the same escaping used in web addresses. The percent sign, slash, question mark and number sign are set aside for future use.

sections.title: Presentation and Transport
sections.content:
The syntax defines the canonical format, and all URN transport and interchange must take place in that format. Applications that know about URNs must offer the option of displaying them in the canonical form so that they can be transcribed directly, for example by cutting and pasting. They may also display a more human-friendly form, using characters that the syntax does not permit, such as replacing the percent notation with real characters in an extended character set.

The appendix on how URL resolvers and browsers handle URNs says that the syntax was defined so that URNs can be used where URLs are expected. A resolver that follows the current URL syntax will extract a scheme value of urn rather than urn followed by the namespace identifier. A URN must be treated as an opaque URL and passed, with its urn tag, to a URN resolver, which may be external or built into the URL resolver. To avoid confusing users, a browser should display the complete URN including the urn tag, so that URN namespace identifiers are not mistaken for URL scheme identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: A URN should always be sent and copied in its canonical form, even if an application can show it more attractively. A program that meets a urn: address should treat the whole thing as one opaque name and pass it to whatever resolves URNs.

sections.title: Lexical and Functional Equivalence
sections.content:
For purposes such as caching, it is often useful to tell whether two URNs are the same without resolving them. The general way to do that is to test for lexical equivalence. Two URNs are lexically equivalent if they are equal octet by octet after three steps of preprocessing: normalise the case of the leading urn token, normalise the case of the namespace identifier, and normalise the case of any percent escaping. Percent escaping must not be removed.

Some namespaces may define extra lexical equivalences, for example a case-insensitive namespace specific string. Any such equivalence must be documented as part of the namespace registration, must always remove some of the false negatives that the general procedure produces, and must never say that two URNs are not equivalent when the general procedure says that they are.

The RFC works through six examples. URN:foo:a123,456, urn:foo:a123,456 and urn:FOO:a123,456 are all lexically equivalent, because the case of the prefix and the namespace identifier does not matter. urn:foo:A123,456 is not equivalent to any of the others, because the case of the namespace specific string does matter. urn:foo:a123%2C456 and URN:FOO:a123%2c456 are equivalent only to each other, because the escaped comma and the literal comma are different octets.

Functional equivalence is a different question, and it is settled by practice within each namespace and managed by the resolvers for that namespace. It is beyond the scope of this document, but namespace registration must include guidance on how to determine functional equivalence, that is, when two URNs are identical within a namespace.
sections.plainLanguage: Two URNs that differ only in the case of the word urn or of the namespace name are the same URN. Two that differ in the case of the rest of the name are not. The escaped and unescaped forms of a character are also different, so the comma and %2C do not match.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document specifies the syntax for URNs. While some namespace resolvers may assign special meaning to certain characters of the namespace specific string, any security consideration resulting from such an assignment is outside the scope of this document. The RFC strongly recommends that the process of registering a namespace identifier include any such considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not assess the security of any particular namespace. It asks whoever registers a namespace to think about it and record the result.
